do_more: Lead with visual paradoxes or absurd contradictions (like the Mug) rather than dry explanations of cognitive biases.
Use concrete, everyday objects (mugs, raincoats) to ground abstract psychology concepts instead of generic scenarios.
Prioritize titles that present a specific, tangible 'thing' or 'situation' over broad questions about brain mechanics.
avoid: Using tech or computer metaphors (e.g., 'tabs open') which seem to underperform compared to physical/prop-based humor.
Focusing on high-relatability but low-visual-impact topics like 'choice overload' or 'sunk cost' without a strong visual anchor.
Relying on standard explanatory hooks; the data suggests the 'what is this weird object?' curiosity gap is stronger.
short.title_style: Use concrete noun phrases that imply a visual contradiction or specific prop (e.g., 'The [Object] Paradox') rather than abstract concept names or questions.
next_tests: Create a 'tight' (30s) version of a top-performing concept (e.g., Mug Paradox) to test if shorter runtime boosts VPD.
Flip a bottom-performing topic (e.g., Sunk Cost) into a visual paradox format and compare performance.
Test a new topic using a non-tech, physical prop metaphor to see if the 'object-first' hook is the actual driver.
